Trans patients often hide their trans status when visiting a doctor if their problem, such as a broken arm, isn't related to their trans status. Transgender people have the right to medical privacy under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). The dialogue in the film "Apollo 13" regarding the backup lunar module pilot, Jack Swigert, is portrayed as untrue by Charles Duke, who was a part of the Apollo 13 mission. Duke stated that Swigert was very familiar with the lunar module as he had also long worked on developing it. The dialogue between ground control and the astronauts was taken nearly verbatim from transcripts and recordings, with the exception of one of the taglines of the film, "Houston, we have a problem." The actual words uttered by Swigert were "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here."

One other incorrect dialogue is after the re-entry blackout. In the film, Tom Hanks (as Lovell) says "Hello Houston... this is Odyssey... it's good to see you again." In the actual re-entry, the Command Module's transmission was finally acquired by a Sikorsky SH-3D Sea King recovery helicopter which then relayed communications to Mission Control. CAPCOM astronaut Joe Kerwin (not Mattingly, who serves as CAPCOM in this scene in the film) then made a call to the spacecraft "Odyssey, Houston standing by. Over." Swigert, not Lovell, replied "Okay, Joe," and unlike the film, this was well before the parachutes deployed; the celebrations depicted at Mission Control were triggered prematurely.

The Cook Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of competitiveness in U.S. congressional districts based on voting patterns in the past two presidential elections. It was first introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy in 1997 and has been updated by The Cook Political Report every two years. The most recent iteration is the 2022 Cook PVI, which uses a formula that weights the most recent presidential election more heavily.

The index looks at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and compares it to the national average. The Cook PVI is displayed as a letter, a plus sign, and a number, with the letter (either a D for Democratic or an R for Republican) indicating the party that won the district and the number showing how many percentage points above the national average it received.

The dialogue in the film "Apollo 13" regarding the backup lunar module pilot, Jack Swigert, is portrayed as untrue by Charles Duke, who was a part of the Apollo 13 mission. Duke stated that Swigert was very familiar with the module as he had also long worked on developing it. The dialogue between ground control and the astronauts was taken nearly verbatim from transcripts and recordings, with the exception of one of the taglines of the film, "Houston, we have a problem." CAPCOM astronaut Joe Kerwin (not Mattingly, who serves as CAPCOM in this scene in the film) then made a call to the spacecraft "Odyssey, Houston standing by. Over." Swigert, not Lovell, replied "Okay, Joe," and unlike the film, this was well before the parachutes deployed; the celebrations depicted at Mission Control were triggered prematurely.

The Cook Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of competitiveness in U.S. politics, based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy in 1997. The index looks at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and compares it to the national average. The Cook PVI is displayed as a letter (either a D for Democratic or an R for Republican), a plus sign, and a number, with the number showing how many percentage points above or below the national average a district received. In 2022, the formula was updated to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily.

In the Old Testament, Zerubbabel, a hero who led the Jews back from Babylon about 520 BC, is mentioned. He was a son of Shealtiel and governed Judah, rebuilding the temple. His lineage is traced in the Book of Chronicles, but there is a discrepancy in the text. The dialogue in the film "Apollo 13" regarding the backup lunar module pilot, Jack Swigert, has been portrayed as untrue by Charles Duke, who was a part of the Apollo 13 mission. Swigert was not portrayed as unprepared for the flight, as he had also worked on developing the lunar module. The dialogue between ground control and the astronauts was taken from transcripts and recordings, with the exception of the famous line, "Houston, we have a problem." In reality, Swigert said, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here."

Another incorrect dialogue is after the re-entry blackout. In the film, Jim Lovell says, "Hello Houston... this is Odyssey... it's good to see you again." In reality, the Command Module's transmission was finally acquired by a Sikorsky SH-3D Sea King recovery helicopter, which then relayed communications to Mission Control. CAPCOM astronaut Joe Kerwin, not Mattingly, made the call to the spacecraft, and Swigert replied, "Okay, Joe," before the parachutes deployed. The celebrations depicted at Mission Control were triggered well before the parachutes deployed.

These inaccuracies in the film's dialogue have been pointed out by various sources, including the BBC's "13 Minutes to the Moon" program and the Smithsonian Channel's "The Real Story: Apollo 13."

Auditory and visual hallucinations are experiences where a person perceives something that is not actually present. In content, for example, people talking about the subject, not speaking to them directly. Like auditory hallucinations, the source of the visual counterpart can also be behind the subject. This can produce a feeling of being looked or stared at, usually with malicious intent. Frequently, auditory hallucinations and their visual counterpart are experienced by the subject together. Hypnagogic hallucinations and hypnopompic hallucinations are considered normal phenomena. Hypnagogic hallucinations can occur as one is falling asleep and hypnopompic hallucinations occur when one is waking up. The Cook Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of competitiveness in U.S. politics, based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy in 1997. The index looks at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and compares it to the national average. The Cook PVI is displayed as a letter (either a D for Democratic or an R for Republican), a plus sign, and a number, with the number showing how many percentage points above or below the national average a district received. In 2022, the formula was updated to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily.

Transgender people face discrimination in healthcare settings, including "trans broken arm syndrome," in which doctors mistakenly assume that a trans person's medical ailments stem from their trans status or gender-affirming care and consequently treat their problem incorrectly or deny them care entirely. Trans patients often hide their trans status when visiting a doctor if their problem, such as a broken arm, isn't related to their trans status. A 2022 survey from the Center for American Progress revealed that 19 percent of trans individuals had experienced this form of discrimination in the past year.

Transgender people have the right to medical privacy under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Medical providers and insurance companies are prohibited from disclosing any personal medical information, including a person's transgender status. HIPAA also allows transgender people to access and receive a copy of their medical records from health care facilities.

It can be difficult for transgender people to find insurance coverage for their medical needs. Even though there is medical consensus that hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery (SRS) are medically necessary for many transgender people, the kinds of health care associated with gender transition are sometimes misunderstood as cosmetic, experimental, or simply unnecessary. This has led to public and private insurance companies denying coverage for such treatment. Courts have repeatedly ruled that these treatments may be medically necessary and have recognized gender dysphoria as a legitimate medical condition constituting a "serious medical need."

The dialogue in the film "Apollo 13" regarding the backup lunar module pilot Jack Swigert and the quote "Houston, we have a problem" is not entirely accurate. According to audio of the air-to-ground communications, the actual words uttered by Swigert were "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here". Ground control responded by saying, "This is Houston. Say again, please." Jim Lovell then repeated, "Houston, we've had a problem."

One other incorrect dialogue is after the re-entry blackout. In the film, Tom Hanks (as Lovell) says "Hello Houston... this is Odyssey... it's good to see you again." In the actual re-entry, the Command Module's transmission was finally acquired by a Sikorsky SH-3D Sea King recovery helicopter which then relayed communications to Mission Control. CAPCOM astronaut Joe Kerwin (not Mattingly, who serves as CAPCOM in this scene in the film) then made a call to the spacecraft "Odyssey, Houston standing by. Over." Swigert, not Lovell, replied "Okay, Joe," and unlike the film, this was well before the parachutes deployed; the celebrations depicted at Mission Control were triggered prematurely.

These inaccuracies in the dialogue were pointed out by Charles Duke, the backup lunar module pilot on the mission, and by astronaut Jack Swigert himself in interviews. The dialogue between ground control and the astronauts was taken nearly verbatim from transcripts and recordings, with the exception of one of the taglines of the film, "Houston, we have a problem." This quote was voted #50 on the list "AFI's 100 Years... 100 Movie Quotes".

The dialogue in the film "Apollo 13" regarding the backup lunar module pilot Jack Swigert and the quote "Houston, we have a problem" is not entirely accurate. According to audio of the air-to-ground communications, the actual words uttered by Swigert were "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here". Ground control responded by saying, "This is Houston. Say again, please." Jim Lovell then repeated, "Houston, we've had a problem."
